The assumption that PRC models remain safely six months behind the American frontier no longer holds in critical areas of national security, particularly cybersecurity. South Korea offers an early warning. Over a matter of days in late September and early October, several of the country’s largest banks and other financial institutions were breached. According to public reports, the attacker used an open- source AI penetration testing tool developed in the PRC, powered by a DeepSeek model and supplemented by others, including the same Zhipu model that NIST identified as the most cyber capable open-weight model released to date. If those reports are correct, these tools allowed a single attacker to carry out multiple intrusions in far less time than a human team would need. The same tools are available to anyone targeting American banks, hospitals, and utilities. A company does not have to adopt a PRC model to become a victim of someone using one. These findings call for a response that distinguishes among developers, capabilities, and uses, with the strongest measures reserved for federal systems and critical infrastructure. The federal government has already begun to act. In October 2026, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) made public an order, issued in July, that excludes DeepSeek products and services from federal civilian agency procurement and requires their removal from agency information systems, including third-party products built on DeepSeek models. That order is an important step, but it reaches only one developer. Other leading PRC developers are subject to the same national security laws, were identified in the same distillation campaigns, and have released models with comparable or greater offensive cyber capability. The federal government should extend the same restrictions to those developers. Our position is straightforward. PRC-developed models should be removed from federal systems, and federal contractors should not use them to perform federal work or handle federal data. They should also be removed from high-risk functions of critical infrastructure, where a compromised or manipulated model could cause physical harm or disrupt essential services. Any exception should be temporary, limited to cases where no trusted substitute yet exists, and approved by DHS, acting through CISA, after an evaluation by the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI). Running a model on American servers keeps data out of the PRC, but it does not change how the model was built, what it was trained to do, or how it behaves under conditions no one thought to test. Across the rest of the economy, the goal is to reduce dependence on PRC models as quickly as trusted American and allied alternatives can replace them. Most companies do not need the most advanced and expensive frontier systems for everyday work, and many turned to PRC models because they perform well at a fraction of the cost. Forcing those companies off PRC models before trusted open-weight alternatives exist would raise their costs and concentrate the market in a small number of closed, proprietary providers. Building those alternatives is not a substitute for restrictions. It is what makes them work. To achieve these goals, the report recommends building a competitive American open-weight ecosystem capable of becoming the global default, model provenance standards to identify what is running inside critical systems, and long- term certainty for the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 (CISA 2015) and the State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program (SLCGP). It also proposes a dedicated DHS channel to share developer-specific threat information with industry, stronger measures to hold those who steal American AI technology accountable, a prohibition on PRC-developed models in federal systems and federal contract work that builds on the action already taken against DeepSeek, a phased prohibition on their use in high-risk functions of critical infrastructure, a bar on using federal cybersecurity grants to buy them, clear guidance that steers critical infrastructure operators toward trusted alternatives, and transition planning now, while the cost of switching remains manageable. There are encouraging signs. American and allied developers are beginning to release more competitive open-weight models, including new models from Reflection AI in the United States and Mistral AI in France released in October

Common sense policy can build on that momentum and help ensure American innovation continues to lead. Congress has too often been behind the curve on emerging technology. As one of our colleagues observed after a briefing on these issues, AI is advancing so quickly that Congress risks being “light years behind.” With this investigation, we intend to narrow that gap. We should not wait five years to discover that much of the world, and much of the United States, runs on AI shaped by the CCP, leaving policymakers with little choice but another costly rip and replace effort. The time to act is now, while we still have the opportunity and leverage to do so. The Foreword’s conclusions are supported by the investigative findings and recommendations that follow. A classified annex accompanies this report and is available to authorized personnel with appropriate security clearances. ______________________________ Andrew R. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

In April 2026, the Committees opened a joint investigation into the national security, cybersecurity, and economic security implications of the growing use of PRC-developed AI models by American companies.1 The investigation focused on why American companies are adopting these models, how PRC developers acquired the capabilities that made them competitive with leading American systems, the role of PRC government support in their development and distribution, and the risks associated with growing American dependence on them.2 As part of that investigation, the Committees examined three U.S. companies (Airbnb, Anysphere, and DoorDash) as case studies of how and why PRC-developed models are already being incorporated into American products and operations.3 • Airbnb runs customized versions of Alibaba’s open-weight Qwen models on U.S.-based service provider infrastructure and uses them in customer support, including for an AI assistant handling roughly 80,000 guest and host interactions per day and a fine-tuned model used to summarize roughly 250,000 support cases and calls each day.4 • Anysphere built Composer 2, the flagship proprietary model in its Cursor coding platform, on a Moonshot AI base model, a fact that became public only after an independent developer identified the underlying model.5 • DoorDash reported that its engineers had downloaded or evaluated PRC- developed models from at least six developers, that 25 PRC model families had been authorized and deployed in a non-trivial manner, which it defined as incurring at least $5,000 in computing and serving costs, and that replacing one PRC-developed model embedded in a larger system could take up to six months, although most of its other uses could be transitioned almost immediately.6 The experiences of Airbnb, Anysphere, and DoorDash are illustrative, not exhaustive. Their representations to the Committees show different ways PRC- developed models are entering American products and operations, but the Committees’ broader investigation found that adoption extends well beyond these three companies and is being driven by forces that are reshaping the wider AI market.7 The investigation produced five main findings: Finding 1. PRC-developed open-weight models are already widely used across the American economy, but much of that use is hard to track. Open- weight models now carry a majority of U.S.-originating traffic on at least one major model marketplace, and PRC models account for most of that volume.8 PRC models also accounted for 41 percent of downloads on the leading open-model repository over the preceding year.9 Because downloaded weights do not require a commercial relationship with the developer, public metrics capture only part of their actual use, and neither customers nor the federal government can reliably see where PRC models are deployed.10 Finding 2. Cost, customization, and near-frontier performance are driving adoption, and the United States lacks a competitive open-weight alternative at the price and performance the market demands. Leading PRC models cost a small fraction of leading American proprietary models at published rates.11 In the most recent independent ranking of open-weight model capability reviewed by the Committees, the highest-ranked American open-weight model placed tenth, behind six PRC models.12 Companies examined by the Committees cited the lack of competitive American open-weight options as a principal reason for their choices.13 Finding 3. Much of the PRC’s apparent progress rests on capabilities extracted from American models, and American data-labeling firms are helping supply the data that trains PRC models. U.S. agencies assessed that six leading PRC developers conducted industrial-scale distillation campaigns against American frontier models, likely with PRC government awareness.14 American data-labeling firms reportedly earn approximately $500 million a year selling American training data to PRC laboratories.15 The Committees assess with high confidence that illicit distillation materially accelerated the development of several PRC model families now used by American companies.16 Finding 4. Beijing is using open-weight distribution, state support, and low prices to expand global dependence on PRC models, while the terms of that dependence are beginning to change. PRC policy documents call for open-source AI with “international influence” and describe the goal of “high-stickiness ecosystem binding.”17 Leading developers sustain heavy losses with support from state funds, state-owned investors, and subsidized compute.18 Developers are now introducing commercial license terms and revenue demands, while Beijing has reportedly considered restricting overseas access to its most advanced models.19 Finding 5. The risks are increasing as PRC models become more capable, while their behavior and security properties can differ in ways ordinary evaluations may not detect. Independent researchers found that some PRC models produced less secure code when prompts referenced politically sensitive topics or a U.S. government user.20 At the same time, NIST and an American frontier developer assessed that Zhipu’s newest open-weight model can autonomously build end-to-end cyber exploits at a level comparable to a leading restricted American model and trails the American frontier by about four months on aggregate government cyber benchmarks.21 Its safeguards were reduced from roughly 95 percent refusal rates to between 3 and 6 percent for an estimated $4,400.22 The Committees’ recommendations are intended to address those findings, build on the action the federal government has already taken against DeepSeek, and strengthen American innovation.23 They are organized around five objectives: Build the American alternative. • Recommendation 1. Launch a national American open-weight AI initiative that pairs public compute, shared evaluation infrastructure, and lawful access to American frontier models for training with anchor demand from federal procurement. • Recommendation 2. Make trusted American AI the global default through export promotion, development finance, and partnerships with allies building sovereign AI capacity. Know which models are running in sensitive systems. • Recommendation 3. Direct NIST, in coordination with DHS through CISA, to develop a model provenance standard and an AI bill of materials, required for federal contractors and high-risk critical infrastructure functions and voluntary elsewhere, with protections for small businesses and open-source developers. • Recommendation 4. Build on the order excluding DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems by prohibiting the use of PRC-developed AI models and their derivatives in federal information systems and in the performance of federal contracts, with a narrow and transparent waiver process for research, testing, and defensive security work, and modernize CISA’s Continuous Diagnostics and Mitigation (CDM) program so agencies can discover and inventory the AI models and agents running on their networks. Prohibit PRC-developed models in high-risk functions of critical infrastructure, with removal schedules tied to the availability of trusted alternatives and temporary exceptions only where none yet exists. Share threat information and strengthen defenses. • Recommendation 5. Enact a long-term reauthorization of CISA 2015 through the Widespread Information Management for the Welfare of Infrastructure and Government (WIMWIG) Act,24 which the Committee on Homeland Security approved unanimously and the House passed as part of the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (H.R. 8800).25 Following enactment of a long-term reauthorization that extends and modernizes CISA 2015 authorities, Congress may consider whether additional narrow clarifications related to sharing information specifically about threats to AI systems are necessary, as those technologies continue to evolve. Complete a long-term reauthorization of the SLCGP through the Protecting Information by Local Leaders for Agency Resilience (PILLAR) Act, which the House passed in November 2025,26 and prohibit the use of program funds for PRC-developed AI models while allowing those funds to be used to replace them. Direct DHS, acting through CISA, to establish a channel for sharing developer-specific AI threat information with industry. • Recommendation 6. Direct NIST’s CAISSI to evaluate leading PRC models on a recurring basis, direct CISA to translate the results into guidance that steers critical infrastructure away from PRC models in sensitive functions, and codify DHS, acting through CISA, as the Sector Risk Management Agency for the Information Technology Sector, including AI models and AI compute infrastructure. • Recommendation 7. Prepare DHS and CISA to defend federal networks and critical infrastructure at machine speed. Establish a DHS pilot program that brings private sector AI and cybersecurity expertise into the Department, with a dedicated allocation for CISA, and direct CISA to serve as the operational lead for securing AI agents on federal civilian networks. • Recommendation 8. Make CISA the single point of submission for AI- related cyber incident reports by building on the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act of 2022 (CIRCIA), which reaches the American entities best positioned to detect incidents involving PRC- developed models, rather than creating new, duplicative reporting requirements. Establish within CISA an independent, nonregulatory board to investigate the root causes of significant cyber incidents and cyber incidents involving AI, including incidents involving foreign adversary models and illicit capability extraction. Impose costs on illicit extraction. • Recommendation 9. Use sanctions, the Entity List, and information and communications technology supply chain authorities against firms engaged in industrial-scale illicit distillation and require identity verification standards that close the gray market of proxy “transfer stations.” • Recommendation 10. Examine the sale of American-produced frontier training data to PRC AI laboratories designated by the U.S. government and consider the imposition of disclosure requirements or export controls. Set durable rules and work with allies. • Recommendation 11. Ensure that federal AI security policy addresses both closed and open models, and establish a federal baseline for AI transparency and security that does not overburden startups, researchers, or nonprofits. • Recommendation 12. Expand joint testing and standards work with allies and direct the Intelligence Community, with DHS, to deliver an assessment of PRC state involvement in open-weight AI strategy.

blocks.text: THE INVESTIGATION

On April 29, 2026, the Chairmen sent letters to Airbnb, Inc. and Anysphere, Inc., the developer of the Cursor AI coding platform, requesting documents, information, and in-person briefings concerning their use of “PRC-developed AI models,” meaning models whose original weights were trained by a company organized, headquartered, or principally operating in the PRC.27 On July 31, 2026, the Chairmen expanded the investigation to DoorDash, Inc.28 The requests focused principally on “open-weight models,”29 whose trained parameters can be downloaded, run, and modified independently of the original developer, and sought information on the models companies used, how they evaluated and deployed them, and their interactions with PRC-based developers.30 Airbnb, Anysphere, and DoorDash responded through written submissions, document productions, and briefings to Committee staff. Airbnb produced materials on its approved generative AI models and how it selects, fine-tunes, and deploys them in customer support, and it later briefed Committee staff.31 DoorDash provided a model inventory, guardrail descriptions, cost data, and internal AI policies, and later briefed Committee staff.32 Anysphere produced a technical report describing the development of its proprietary coding model and also briefed staff.33 Across the three companies, the Committees examined both how the models were selected and used and whether they were run on company- controlled infrastructure or accessed through services operated by the original developer.34 The companies’ representations reflected different forms of adoption, from direct use in customer support systems to the use of PRC-developed models as components of proprietary products. The Committees supplemented the company materials with public hearings, classified briefings, closed-door roundtables, and other research on the broader development and security of PRC AI models. The Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection held hearings in December 2025, March 2026, and June 2026 on AI-enabled cyber threats, PRC-developed AI and robotics, and the security implications of frontier models, agentic AI, and AI coding tools.36 Subcommittee staff then traveled to Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan in August 2026 to engage with representatives of host governments and private sector leaders on AI adoption and governance, cybersecurity constraints, supply chain risks, and critical infrastructure resilience. Select Committee staff also traveled to Silicon Valley, Singapore, Malaysia, and Vietnam to examine the broader ecosystem supporting PRC AI development and overseas deployment, including access to advanced compute, cloud and data center infrastructure, and the channels through which those capabilities reach foreign markets. Staff from both Committees received classified briefings from leading American frontier AI developers and met with federal agencies, cybersecurity companies, AI laboratories, and researchers.37 The Committees also examined how PRC developers acquired the capabilities that made their models competitive with American alternatives. That inquiry included “distillation,” a common training technique in which outputs from one model are used to train another, and alleged large-scale efforts by PRC developers to extract capabilities from American frontier systems.38 In this report, “illicit distillation” refers to unauthorized, large-scale extraction through methods such as fraudulent accounts, proxy networks, or violations of a developer’s terms of service.39 American AI Models (Apr. 23, 2026), https://perma.cc/P6U3-SQMD [hereinafter NSTM-4].

blocks.text: FINDINGS

Multiple independent data sources show that American use of PRC- developed open-weight models has grown rapidly. On OpenRouter, the share of tokens from U.S.-originating requests directed to open-weight models rose from 26 percent in September 2025 to 60 percent in August 2026, with models from PRC laboratories accounting for most of that volume.40 A separate analysis found that PRC models accounted for more than 30 percent of weekly token consumption by American companies on the platform beginning in February 2026, peaking at 46 percent, up from 4.5 percent during the first half of 2025.41 PRC-developed models also accounted for 41 percent of downloads on Hugging Face over the preceding year.42 Alibaba’s Qwen family alone had more than 151,000 derivative models on the platform, and its share of new open-model fine-tunes and adaptations rose from 1 percent in January 2024 to 69 percent by February 2026.43 One leading venture capital firm observed that a majority of American AI startups appear to use PRC open weights somewhere in their technology stack.44 Spending data, however, can drastically understate how widely these models are used. In May 2026, DeepSeek models accounted for 17 percent of tokens processed through one major developer platform’s AI gateway but only about 1 percent of spending.45 A December 2025 survey of enterprise AI spending similarly found that PRC open models represented only about 1 percent of enterprise large language model application programming interface (API) usage.46 The reason is simple: once weights are downloaded and run on private infrastructure, continued use may generate little or no commercial activity that can be measured.47 The companies examined by the Committees illustrate the point. Neither Airbnb nor DoorDash had paid a PRC developer or maintained a commercial agreement with one.48 Each reported running PRC-developed models on infrastructure in the United States, substantially reducing the risk that user data is transmitted directly to the PRC, and DoorDash reported that it also blocks connections to PRC-based AI services from its corporate devices and model hosting environments.49 But the absence of a commercial relationship does not mean the technology is no longer in use. There may be no contract, invoice, ongoing vendor relationship, or other conventional record showing that dependence. Model lineage, or the chain of models and training steps from which a model descends, can become even harder to see as weights are modified and reused. Fine- tuning, continued pretraining, merging, and distillation can progressively obscure a model’s origin, allowing PRC-developed weights or capabilities to be modified and repackaged until it is no longer obvious that the resulting product was PRC- developed.50 Anysphere, for example, built Cursor’s flagship Composer 2 model on a PRC-developed base model, a fact that became public only after an outside developer identified the underlying model.51 Researchers have shown that upstream model relationships can remain technically detectable after post-training and release under a different name, but identifying them requires the right tools and disclosure practices.52 Today, however, no standard requires that lineage to be disclosed. An American-branded application, cloud service, or industrial system may therefore depend on a PRC-developed model several layers beneath what a customer sees. That visibility gap becomes especially important when something goes wrong. If a serious vulnerability, hidden behavior, or disruption affected a widely used PRC model family, weak lineage records could make it difficult to determine which downstream products inherited the problem. The same problem would arise if future releases, security updates, or other parts of the model ecosystem became unavailable. Without reliable provenance records, neither customers nor the federal government can readily identify where PRC-developed models and their derivatives are operating or how far a problem could spread. The companies examined by the Committees generally selected models based on performance, cost, latency, and flexibility. Airbnb Chief Executive Officer Brian Chesky publicly explained that the company relied on Alibaba’s model because it was “fast and cheap.”53 Representations made to the Committees similarly showed that Airbnb, Anysphere, and DoorDash viewed PRC-developed open-weight models as competitive options in their own right, not substitutes of last resort.54 Price is a major part of that appeal. AI developers generally charge based on how much text a model reads and generates, measured in “tokens,” or small pieces of words and characters. These figures do not adjust for differences in capability or for caching, batch discounts, promotions, or self- hosting costs, but they illustrate the scale of the price gap that companies face when deciding which models to deploy. Companies can fine-tune models on their own data, adjust their behavior, run them on infrastructure they control, and reduce dependence on a single vendor that could change terms or cut off access.58 Airbnb rated open- weight candidates as offering “full flexibility” for fine-tuning, compared with “limited flexibility” for proprietary alternatives.59 DoorDash similarly told the Committees that open-weight models “reduce the risk a single developer could change or turn off access to a model without notice.”60 That flexibility can matter in practice. In July 2026, after one American model under evaluation exploited a weakness in its testing environment and breached the network of Hugging Face, the company reported that American frontier models refused to assist with parts of the defensive response because their safeguards could not distinguish a defender from an attacker.61 Hugging Face instead used Zhipu’s open-weight GLM-5.2 model to complete portions of the work.62 The episode illustrates why companies and cybersecurity researchers may value models they can run and modify themselves, even when those models raise separate national security concerns. PRC-developed models are also increasingly capable. DoorDash’s internal benchmark, DashBench, measured how well paired AI models identified real problems in 105 historical code changes. A configuration pairing Moonshot’s Kimi K2.6 with an American frontier model achieved the highest score of any configuration tested, outperforming pairings built on leading American open- weight models by more than 20 percentage points.63 Table 3 summarizes those results. The company stated that these evaluations do not determine which models it adopts.64 Market-wide benchmarks highlight this rapid convergence. The highest- ranked American open-weight model now sits at tenth place in the latest Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, an independent ranking that measures overall capability across reasoning, knowledge, mathematics, coding, and agentic tasks, trailing six PRC models.65 While PRC systems have lagged American frontier models by roughly seven months on average since 2023, rapid releases from DeepSeek, Moonshot, Alibaba, and Zhipu have dramatically narrowed that lead across several core domains.66 That narrowing gap is changing how companies deploy AI. Rather than choosing between an American model and a PRC-developed model, companies increasingly use different models for different tasks. Airbnb described a portfolio approach in which “no single LLM can efficiently serve all” of its support use cases,67 while DoorDash described routing some work to a PRC-developed model and more difficult tasks to an American model.68 Companies also described controls that treat model outputs as untrusted and subject them to additional review.69 Those controls can reduce the risk of a bad output causing harm, but they do not answer other questions, including where a model came from, how it may behave under different conditions, or what happens if access to it is disrupted. Using several models at once can also make it harder to know which model handled a particular task or had access to particular data. For American companies, the larger problem is the limited supply of competitive domestic open-weight models near the frontier. DoorDash cited the lack of competitive American open-weight alternatives as a principal reason for using PRC-developed models and described American open-weight models as “a strategic asset for U.S. competitiveness and security.”70 In the September 2026 Artificial Analysis ranking, the highest-ranked American open-weight model, Thinking Machines Lab’s Inkling, placed behind six PRC models.71 Thinking Machines Lab also disclosed that Inkling’s initial training used synthetic data generated by other open-weight models, including Moonshot’s Kimi K2.5.72 That means even some American efforts to build alternatives are still drawing on PRC- developed models. One reason American alternatives remain limited is that U.S. developers are playing by a different set of rules. Training frontier models is expensive, and American companies generally rely on proprietary access to recover those costs rather than releasing their strongest models as open weights.73 They also cannot lawfully replicate the distillation campaigns described in Finding 3, which used fraudulent accounts and proxy networks to extract capabilities from competing American models in violation of provider restrictions.74 PRC developers, meanwhile, benefit from state investment and subsidized compute.75 The result is an uneven playing field in which American companies bear the cost of developing frontier capabilities, while PRC firms can use those capabilities, backed by state support, to bring cheaper open-weight models to market. There are signs that American open-weight developers, including Meta, NVIDIA, Thinking Machines Lab, Arcee AI, Poolside, and Reflection AI, are starting to catch up.76 For example, on October 5, 2026, Reflection AI released Beam, which it says matches leading PRC open models on advanced reasoning benchmarks while using substantially less inference compute, although those claims have not yet been independently verified.77 Allied developers are advancing as well. In October 2026, France-based Mistral AI launched Mistral Large 4, which the company says ranks among the strongest open-weight models available and outperforms PRC models in certain areas, including cyber.78 On the policy side, the Administration’s AI Action Plan calls for a “supportive environment for open models” aimed at making American models global standards.79 The PRC’s gains have occurred despite U.S. controls intended to restrict access to the most advanced semiconductors.80 Some analysts argue that those constraints pushed PRC developers toward more efficient architectures and open- weight distribution.81 However, export controls were only part of the story. U.S. government agencies and American frontier developers found that several leading PRC AI labs also accelerated their models by extracting capabilities from American systems, while at least one developer obtained advanced American chips it was not authorized to acquire.82 By early 2026, those extraction campaigns were operating at industrial scale. In February 2026, American frontier developers disclosed that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, and MiniMax had collectively generated more than 16 million exchanges with American AI systems through approximately 24,000 fraudulent accounts.83 In April 2026, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) described the broader activity as “deliberate, industrial-scale campaigns,” principally originating from the PRC, to distill American frontier AI systems.84 OSTP also warned that developers could use the resulting models to reproduce Plan]. The joint advisory identified DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun, and Z.ai, the international brand of Zhipu, as participants in large-scale extraction campaigns involving billions of tokens from American frontier systems, likely with PRC government awareness, and described distillation as “the core” of the development strategy of several leading PRC AI labs.88 The advisory also concluded that DeepSeek’s widely cited $5.6 million training-cost figure was “misleading” because it excluded the value of data acquired through distillation.89 An American frontier developer found that a distilled model can acquire dangerous capabilities, including in biological and cyber domains, even when the harvested exchanges contain little information about those subjects, while safeguards limiting misuse of the original model “do not transfer” to the distilled model.90 The same developer reported that Zhipu employees stopped trying to distill the cyber capabilities of one American model after its safeguards interfered with the requested attacks, then shifted to other American models they believed had weaker protections.91 Those extracted capabilities are not confined to commercial use, as discussed further in Finding 4. PRC developers are also obtaining American training data through ordinary commercial relationships.92 Reporting in August 2026 found that leading PRC AI laboratories collectively pay U.S. data vendors, including Surge AI, Mercor, AfterQuery, and Turing, roughly $500 million a year for expert reasoning, coding, evaluation, and other training data.93 Some of those vendors also serve American frontier laboratories and the U.S. Army and Air Force, while reported PRC customers include Tencent, ByteDance, Alibaba, Ant Group, and Moonshot.94 At least one U.S. data company reportedly declined a ByteDance contract over national security concerns, while another does not sell outside the United States.95 The Committees do not suggest that these sales are currently unlawful. They do, however, raise a separate policy question of whether American expert training data, including data from firms serving U.S. defense customers, should remain available without restriction to PRC laboratories designated by the U.S. government as military companies or placed on the Entity List.96 PRC developers are drawing on American resources through two separate channels. Illicit distillation transfers capabilities directly from American frontier models, while commercial purchases provide the high-quality data used to train and refine PRC systems. Both shorten the path to models that can compete with American systems. 95 Id. Finding 4. Open-weight distribution is a deliberate PRC strategy to expand global dependence, backed by state policy and capital, and the monetization phase has begun. The PRC has made open-weight distribution central to its effort to expand the global reach and influence of its AI ecosystem. The rapid international adoption described above suggests that the strategy is gaining traction outside the PRC.97 PRC policy documents call for an open-source AI ecosystem with “international influence,” while researchers at a state academy have described the approach as pairing “low-cost technology exports” with “high-stickiness ecosystem binding.”98 A 2025 article published by the Cyberspace Administration of China urged PRC developers to “attract global developers to participate in technological iteration” and increase Beijing’s “international discourse power over technical rules.”99 The National Office for Philosophy and Social Sciences went further, arguing that open-source community rules could shape the “underlying structure” of global AI governance and urging the PRC to “substantively intervene in and shape” those rules.100 In July 2026, Xi Jinping also endorsed open-source AI, calling for “open-source, openness, collaboration and sharing” in AI.101 That direction from Beijing is already reflected in the strategies and public commitments of leading PRC AI developers. Moonshot AI describes open-weight models as the foundation of a “broad and open ecosystem,”102 while DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng has said that the company’s “strongest model will probably also be open sourced.”103 Zhipu founder Tang Jie released GLM-5.2 under the permissive MIT license, arguing that “true safety is not built on technological closure and barriers.”104 Alibaba’s chief executive likewise pledged to keep Qwen open-source and to turn it into the “operating system of the AI era.”105 The PRC has committed substantial state financing to support this strategy. In January 2025, the PRC established an $8.2 billion106 National AI Industry Investment Fund backed by state investors,107 while the state-owned Bank of China announced plans to provide approximately $138 billion in AI-related financing over five years.108 Leading model developers have also benefited from direct subsidies, state investment, and government ownership: • Alibaba received approximately $1.05 billion in company-wide government grants in fiscal year 2024,109 while Hangzhou separately awarded Alibaba DAMO Academy about $4.7 million specifically for Qwen.110 • Zhipu disclosed at least $13.8 million in AI-related R&D subsidies, received a $29.8 million state investment, and is 4.9 percent owned by government bodies, with another 3.5 percent held by Tsinghua University.111 • DeepSeek received roughly $146.2 million from China’s National AI Industry Investment Fund in 2026.112 • MiniMax reported about $2.3 million in deferred government grants at the end of 2025,113 with an additional, undisclosed amount of state capital provided through multiple financing rounds led by Shanghai state-capital firms.114 • Moonshot is 18.1 percent indirectly owned by eighteen Chinese government bodies through investment funds and partnerships.115 • ByteDance has a 1 percent “golden share” in its key China operating entity held by Beijing through WangTou Zhongwen (Beijing) Technology Co., Ltd.116 Annex B documents additional provincial, municipal, and district subsidies for compute, deployment, taxes, talent, and customer adoption. Together, these programs reduce the costs of developing and commercializing PRC AI models. The scale of financial losses reported by leading developers illustrates the scale of investment required to compete. When Zhipu and MiniMax listed in Hong Kong in January 2026, Zhipu disclosed approximately $330 million in losses on $27 million in revenue during the first half of 2025, while MiniMax reported $512 million in losses on $53 million in revenue during the first nine months.117 Independent analysts nevertheless identify private technology firms as the primary drivers of PRC AI progress, with state support most effective when directed toward those firms.118 Government financing and subsidies give 118 Chan et al., supra note 18. developers greater latitude to absorb losses, lower prices, and prioritize market share over near-term profitability. The relationship between leading developers and the PRC state also extends beyond financing. Several have roots in research networks connected to state security and intelligence institutions, with some ties continuing through cybersecurity partnerships. Zhipu, for example, traces part of its research origins to a Tsinghua University project with ties to the PRC intelligence apparatus.119 In 2017, Zhipu co-founder Li Juanzi led a National Natural Science Foundation of China project on person profiling and data analysis under a joint fund with the China General Technology Research Institute, an entity that supports the Ministry of State Security’s (MSS) technical espionage capabilities.120 Tsinghua identified XLORE 2.0 and NewsMiner as outputs of the project, designed to analyze “China- related key persons and events.”121 The project drew on Tsinghua’s Knowledge Engineering Group (KEG) and involved researchers who later joined Zhipu,122 including co-founder Tang Jie,123 CEO Zhang Peng,124 and researchers Xin Lv and Zijun Yao.125 Moonshot AI founder Yang Zhilin also emerged from Tsinghua’s KEG, where he conducted research under Tang Jie with support from government projects focused on “public security and social management.”126 He later contributed to Zhipu’s GLM model lineage through the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence and, through his company Recurrent AI, collaborated with Huawei Cloud to develop the PanGu NLP model using computing resources from Peng Cheng Laboratory.127 Additional information points to contacts between Zhipu and elements of the PRC’s military cyber apparatus, as detailed further in Annex A.128 Zhipu and Alibaba Cloud also participate in the PRC’s government cybersecurity and vulnerability-reporting systems. In April 2026, a Zhipu executive participated in the launch of the National Artificial Intelligence Security Vulnerability Database, established under the China National Vulnerability Database of Information Security, which is maintained by the MSS’s 13th Bureau.129 Zhipu subsequently reported vulnerabilities identified through its GLM models to the database.130 Alibaba Cloud has also maintained longstanding ties to the PRC’s national cybersecurity apparatus. In 2019, the National Computer Network Emergency Response Technical Team/Coordination Center of China designated Alibaba Cloud a national-level cybersecurity emergency service support unit alongside firms including Qihoo 360 and NSFOCUS.131 In 2021, PRC regulators suspended Alibaba Cloud from a government threat-sharing platform for disclosing the Log4j vulnerability to the Apache Software Foundation before notifying PRC authorities.132 U.S. government designations and intelligence assessments have also raised concerns about the military and intelligence ties of leading PRC AI developers. The Department of War designated Alibaba a Chinese military company in June 2026, while Zhipu has been on the Commerce Department’s Entity List since January 2025.133 A senior U.S. official stated that DeepSeek “has willingly provided and will likely continue to provide support to China’s military and intelligence operations,” citing more than 150 procurement records involving the PLA and entities affiliated with the PRC defense industrial base, along with technology services provided to PLA research institutions.134 The Committees’ review of PLA procurement records likewise identified military applications involving several PRC AI model families, including: • A 2026 procurement sought servers for an “intelligent command information system” and required support for the full development workflow of Alibaba’s Qwen and DeepSeek models.135 • A 2026 cyber range procurement required integrating DeepSeek to support “intelligent attack” and “intelligent penetration.”136 • A 2026 model-upgrade project required DeepSeek, Qwen, Moonshot’s Kimi, and MiniMax models to operate entirely on an internal network without internet access for military AI agent and software development applications.137 • A 2026 military medical procurement called for locally deploying DeepSeek or Qwen to support medical record generation, quality control, and clinical decision support.138 • A 2024 procurement called for deploying and fine-tuning Zhipu’s GLM models on a military office network.139 These records show PRC-developed models being incorporated into PLA computing environments and operational workflows, including through purchases of servers, software platforms, and local deployment infrastructure configured around specific model families. Additional procurements for integrated foundation model platforms and dedicated local deployment infrastructure show that this use extends beyond the examples above.140 The same state-backed ecosystem that supports these models at home is also helping them gain adoption abroad, creating a separate risk that low-cost access today becomes dependence tomorrow.141 There are already signs that PRC developers are seeking to convert adoption into commercial leverage. Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 license requires model-as-a-service providers with more than $20 million in annual revenue to negotiate a separate commercial agreement with the company.142 Alibaba reportedly plans to charge large commercial users of its next Qwen release, while Moonshot AI was reportedly seeking up to 30 percent of revenue generated from Kimi K3 services offered through major American cloud providers.143 Dependence on a PRC model family could also leave users exposed to decisions made in Beijing. In July 2026, Reuters reported that PRC authorities, in meetings led by the Ministry of Commerce, had discussed restricting overseas access to the country’s most advanced AI models, including Alibaba’s Qwen and Zhipu’s GLM-5.2.144 For American companies that build products around a PRC model family, this creates a continuity risk controlled not only by the developer but also by the PRC government. Even if previously downloaded weights remain available, companies could lose access to future releases, security updates, or improvements. DoorDash’s estimate that replacing a single PRC-developed model embedded in a larger system could take up to six months illustrates how quickly technical adoption can become operational dependence.145 That dependence would not be limited to the United States. A January 2026 Microsoft analysis found that DeepSeek had gained meaningful market share across a number of developing countries, including shares of roughly 11 to 14 percent in several African markets and substantially higher shares in countries including Belarus, Cuba, and Russia.146 Wider adoption of PRC-developed models abroad would extend the same dependency questions to foreign governments, companies, and digital ecosystems with which American firms interact. These dynamics complicate the U.S. policy response. As Findings 2 and 3 show, the United States does not yet have a comparably competitive open-weight ecosystem, while PRC developers have also benefited from capabilities extracted from American frontier models.147 Policymakers therefore face the challenge of reducing dependence on PRC-developed models while managing the cost of replacing tools on which American companies have already come to rely. In July 2026, after the release of Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, administration officials publicly raised concerns about illicit distillation and unauthorized access to advanced American chips, while press reports indicated that restrictions on PRC-developed models were under consideration.148 The Secretary of the Treasury warned that “open source is not open season on American IP” and indicated that sanctions remained possible.149 At the same time, administration officials continued to support a competitive ecosystem that includes open-weight models.150 In October 2026, DHS made public an order, issued in July under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018, that excludes DeepSeek products and services from federal civilian agency procurement and requires agencies to remove them from their information systems, including third-party products and services built using DeepSeek.151 The order does not apply to private use or to Department of War systems.152 Microsoft Report Says, Associated Press (Jan. 8, 2026). Industry warned against broad restrictions. Nearly 200 startups and technology companies urged the administration not to cut off access to PRC open- weight models, arguing that many young companies had already become dependent on them.153 That figure likely understates the scale of U.S. industry exposure. As Finding 1 explains, open-weight models can be downloaded, modified, and embedded without an ongoing commercial relationship or other conventional record of use, making much of that dependence difficult to detect. The number of American companies relying directly or indirectly on PRC- developed models may therefore be substantially larger than public disclosures suggest, and a disruption in access to future releases, updates, or related services could impose costs across a much broader segment of the American economy. Major American technology companies separately cautioned against “premature restrictions,” emphasizing the value of capable open models for innovation and cybersecurity.154 The resulting policy challenge is how to reduce that dependence quickly while ensuring that trusted American and allied open-weight alternatives are available to replace what is removed. Independent testing indicates that constraints introduced during development can persist in ways that conventional performance benchmarks may not reveal. CrowdStrike found that DeepSeek’s flagship reasoning model was up to 50 percent more likely to produce code with severe security flaws when a prompt referenced topics the CCP considers politically sensitive.155 Booz Allen Hamilton found that, in more than 2,800 trials, three of four PRC models it tested produced significantly more vulnerable code when the user identified as a member of the U.S. government, and that the vulnerabilities were highly obfuscated.156 NIST found that DeepSeek models echoed CCP narratives four times as often as American reference models and were far more susceptible to hijacking in agent workflows.157 CrowdStrike concluded that the behavior it observed was more likely an unintended consequence of training the model to adhere to CCP political requirements, like “Core Socialist Values.”158 The security consequence is nevertheless the same. A model can perform normally on standard evaluations yet degrade under conditions that a user may not know to test.159 154 Bellan, Industry Urges Against Broad Open-Weight Restrictions, supra note 62. The stakes have also increased as PRC open-weight models have become more capable. In November 2025, an American frontier developer disclosed that a group it assessed with high confidence to be a PRC state-sponsored actor had used its AI system in a largely autonomous cyber espionage campaign against approximately 30 targets, with AI agents performing most of the intrusion activity.160 The Committee on Homeland Security responded with oversight letters and a December 2025 hearing.161 Committee Members and staff later received classified briefings on advanced cyber-capable models and the risks posed by jailbroken systems.162 Then, in April 2026, the same developer announced Mythos Preview, a model capable of autonomously discovering and exploiting serious vulnerabilities in critical software. It concluded that the capability was too dangerous for general release and limited access to selected cyber defenders.163 Five months later, NIST and the developer separately concluded that Zhipu’s openly available GLM-5.3 had reached comparable offensive cyber capability in important respects.164 NIST described GLM-5.3 as capable of autonomously building end-to-end cyber exploits and found that it trailed the American frontier by only about four months on an aggregate of government cyber benchmarks.165 Because the model’s weights are public, researchers were able to reduce its refusal rate on harmful requests from approximately 95 percent to between 3 and 6 percent using roughly 2,200 hours of graphics processor time at an estimated cost of about $4,400.166 The same American developer warned that the advanced cyber capabilities it had restricted in April “have now arrived” in open weights.167 The progression from AI-assisted intrusion activity to downloadable models capable of autonomous exploit development sharply reduces the time between the emergence of a frontier capability and its broad availability. Deployment architecture changes some of these risks, but not all of them. The companies that the Committees examined largely avoided sending data to PRC- operated services by running models on their own infrastructure or through U.S.- based cloud and inference providers.168 Those deployment choices substantially reduce the most direct form of data exposure. They do not, however, resolve the broader provenance and dependency risks described in Findings 1 and 4, or change how the underlying model was trained and aligned. [hereinafter Anthropic Espionage Disclosure]. supra note 21. Users who access PRC models through PRC-operated services face additional risks. Requests sent to those services may place prompts, proprietary documents, and personal data on infrastructure controlled by PRC companies subject to PRC intelligence and data security laws.169 At scale, those interactions can create an intelligence collection opportunity across American industry, research, and government.170 Recent evidence illustrates how those risks can materialize. In September 2026, an American frontier developer reported that PRC laboratories had silently relayed customer requests to third parties, including sessions originating from routing services used in the United States and Europe that contained names, email addresses, company information, and other sensitive data.171 The Select Committee separately found that DeepSeek transmitted American user data to the PRC through infrastructure connected to state-owned China Mobile.172 Exposure can also persist through the personnel, affiliates, and services surrounding a deployment. Airbnb retained a PRC office focused on product development after winding down its domestic lodging business there in 2022, and current job listings indicate that its PRC-based team develops AI for customer service, including fine-tuning and evaluating large language models.173 The company disclosed in 2021 that PRC government agencies may require or request that it share information about users who use or offer services in the PRC through its platform.174 According to Airbnb, its PRC-based employees have access only to a limited subset of Airbnb-approved models, and its AI models do not send user data or related information to any PRC-based entity for processing.175 The Committees have not established whether PRC-based personnel evaluate, fine- tune, deploy, or maintain the PRC-developed models identified in Airbnb’s production, or whether they can access data about users outside the PRC processed by those systems.176 Large technology companies have greater capacity to mitigate some of these risks through extensive testing, fine-tuning, and layered deployment controls. DoorDash described treating model inputs, outputs, and proposed actions as untrusted, validating model files with cryptographic hashes, permitting only secure file formats, and relying on overlapping guardrails.177 Airbnb described a cross-functional review process and additional safety checks for customer-facing (adopted June 10, 2021, effective Sept. 1, 2021), https://perma.cc/83KP-5W5P. 175 Airbnb Nov. 13 Email, supra note 4; see also Airbnb Briefing, supra note 31; Airbnb Response, supra note 31, at 2–4. 176 Airbnb Briefing, supra note 31. deployments.178 Smaller downstream users may lack dedicated AI security teams, the resources to conduct extensive adversarial testing, or the expertise to identify context-triggered behavior.179 CrowdStrike cautioned that generic open-source benchmarks are insufficient and recommended testing AI-coding assistants within the environments in which they will actually operate.180 Those controls, however, do not substitute for evaluating the developer itself. The companies’ submissions reflected substantial attention to model performance, deployment architecture, and security controls.181 Airbnb described reviews covering security, privacy, legal, and open-source licensing.182 DoorDash stated that it “never assumes a model is ‘safe’ or ‘secure’” and described controls for validating model provenance and integrity.183 Anysphere described a vendor risk management program and technical controls governing infrastructure and model access.184 Their submissions provided considerably less detail about how they evaluated the PRC developers themselves.185 When the White House publicly accused Moonshot AI of illicitly distilling an American model and acquiring restricted chips, DoorDash told the Committees that it had no independent knowledge of the allegations, that the public disclosures did not provide enough information to identify specific security risks from its use of the model, and that it had not changed the deployment, permissions, or security monitoring of the Moonshot model it uses.186 Airbnb also continued to list Alibaba models as approved for production use after the Department of War identified Alibaba as a Chinese military company, though the designation itself did not prohibit U.S. companies from using Alibaba’s models.187 By contrast, Anysphere informed the Committees that it plans to explore phasing out PRC-developed open-weight models because of geopolitical risk.188 Those differences reflect a broader information problem. Model-level testing can identify how a system behaves under the conditions tested. Developer-level diligence addresses different questions, including how the model was developed, what legal obligations shaped that process, what institutions supported it, and what risks may have been introduced upstream. The federal government currently lacks a dedicated channel for delivering developer-specific AI threat information to industry, while the principal federal cybersecurity information-sharing statute 181 Airbnb June 30 Email, supra note 31; DoorDash Response, supra note 6; DoorDash Production, supra note 6, attachs. B, D. 184 Cursor Security Page, supra note 168. has operated under short-term extensions since its original authorization expired in September 2025.189 Together, the evidence shows that secure deployment is necessary but not sufficient. Self-hosting can reduce direct data exposure, and layered controls can reduce operational risk, but neither resolves risks arising from model behavior, rapidly proliferating capabilities, developer provenance, or the legal and institutional environment in which the model was produced. Those risks become more consequential as PRC-developed open-weight models approach the capabilities of the most advanced American systems.

blocks.text: RECOMMENDATIONS

The findings above present a familiar policy problem. Capable, low-cost PRC technology can become deeply embedded before the United States has competitive alternatives or a practical plan to unwind that dependence. The experiences with Huawei, ZTE, and DJI show the costs of waiting until dependence is already entrenched.190 Open-weight AI presents many of the same challenges, but with an important difference. Model weights can be copied, modified, and embedded in downstream products in ways that are far harder to inventory or remove than physical equipment. Table 5. Comparing PRC Technology Dependencies Huawei and ZTE DJI PRC Open-Weight AI Models Why users adopted it Low-cost, capable telecom equipment Low-cost, capable drones Low-cost, capable, customizable models When concern emerged 2012: House Intelligence Committee warning 2017–2025: Growing federal security restrictions 2026: White House and joint federal warnings What happened next 2020: Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act and removal program 2025: Addition to FCC Covered List (December 2025) Under consideration How entrenched dependence became Equipment remained embedded in rural networks DJI remained widely used by public-safety and commercial users Full scale is unknown Cost of unwinding Est. $4.98 billion Est. 6× higher average replacement cost Unknown and growing Sources: Committees’ analysis.191 Dependence becomes harder and more expensive to unwind when there are no viable alternatives available. In 2012, the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence recommended that American companies avoid Huawei and ZTE equipment because of national security concerns.192 Many small and rural providers nevertheless continued to rely on that equipment because it was affordable, reliable, and difficult to replace at comparable cost.193 Congress later enacted the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019 to fund removal and replacement.194 By then, however, the estimated cost had reached approximately $4.98 billion, far exceeding the original $1.9 billion appropriation and leaving a $3.08 billion shortfall.195 Congress authorized additional funding in December 2024, more than a decade after the original warning, and removal remained incomplete.196 The experience with DJI illustrates a related problem. Dependence is hardest to unwind when users have few viable substitutes. After the Department of the Interior restricted its own use of foreign-made drones, the average cost of compliant replacements rose from about $2,600 to more than $15,000 per drone, nearly six times the prior average.197 Public safety agencies nationwide, including state and local law enforcement, and small businesses likewise resisted broader restrictions on DJI because lower-cost domestic alternatives were not yet available at comparable scale or capability.198 Recent reporting describes similar challenges as American companies seek to replace PRC components in robotics and other industries.199 Dependence on AI systems can be far harder to unwind. Unlike telecommunications equipment or drones, models can be copied, modified, embedded several layers deep in other products, and run anywhere, making even their use difficult to inventory. Hardware restrictions can be enforced at the border or through equipment authorization.200 No comparable chokepoint exists for open weights. The lesson from Huawei, ZTE, and DJI is therefore to build competitive alternatives, establish visibility, and plan for substitution before dependence becomes too costly to unwind.

blocks.text: A. Build the American Alternative

Recommendation 1. Launch a national American open-weight AI initiative. The most effective response to inexpensive PRC models is a competitive American alternative. That alternative is also what will make broader restrictions on PRC- developed models workable. Startups, technology companies, and cybersecurity firms have warned that they lack American or allied open-weight models with comparable price and performance, and that removing PRC models without those alternatives in place would raise costs and concentrate the market in a small number of closed, proprietary providers.201 Recent releases from Reflection AI and Mistral AI show that the gap is beginning to close.202 Congress should authorize, and the executive branch should establish, a public-private initiative to accelerate the development of frontier competitive American open-weight models. The initiative should include an interagency coordination body, access to public computing resources for qualified American developers and researchers, a shared testbed and evaluation infrastructure, and an open-weight AI challenge to accelerate talent and research. DHS, through CISA, should participate in the shared testbed so that the security of American open-weight models, including their resistance to misuse against critical infrastructure, is evaluated alongside their performance. The initiative should also explore a structured framework under which American frontier developers may voluntarily license model outputs to qualified American open-weight developers for training, giving American firms a lawful path to the kind of capability transfer that PRC developers have obtained illicitly.203 Federal agencies should serve as anchor customers for secure American open-weight models where appropriate. These efforts would advance the AI Action Plan’s call for a supportive environment for open models.204 Recommendation 2. Make trusted American AI the global default. The executive branch should use export promotion, development finance, and diplomatic engagement to help partner nations adopt trusted American AI, including open-weight models suitable for sovereign deployment. This effort should prioritize countries where PRC models are gaining market share and should coordinate with allied governments that are developing their own AI capacity.205

blocks.text: B. Know What Is Running

Recommendation 3. Establish a model provenance standard and an AI bill of materials. Congress should direct NIST, in coordination with DHS through CISA, to develop a standard for documenting the lineage of AI models, including base models, significant fine-tuning, and distillation sources, and a machine- readable AI bill of materials that identifies the models embedded in a product or service. The standard should be required for federal contractors and for AI used in high-risk functions of critical infrastructure, and voluntary elsewhere. NIST should also support research into technical methods for verifying model lineage.206 Requirements should be scaled to minimize burdens on startups, researchers, and open-source developers. Recommendation 4. Extend federal restrictions beyond DeepSeek, keep PRC-developed AI models out of federal contract work and high-risk functions of critical infrastructure, and give agencies the visibility to enforce these restrictions. The executive branch has already taken an important step. DHS has ordered federal civilian agencies to exclude DeepSeek products and services from procurement and to remove them from agency information systems, including third-party products built using DeepSeek.207 Congress has separately prohibited DeepSeek on intelligence community systems.208 These actions reach one developer. Other leading PRC developers are subject to the same PRC laws, were identified in the same distillation campaigns, and have released openly available models with comparable or greater offensive cyber capability.209 DHS and the Federal Acquisition Security Council should evaluate those developers for comparable orders. Congress should prohibit federal agencies from using AI models developed by entities subject to the jurisdiction or control of the PRC, including derivatives of those models, in federal information systems. The No Adversarial AI Act, which was introduced in June 2025, would move in this direction by requiring the Federal Acquisition Security Council to maintain a public list of AI developed by foreign adversaries and directing agencies to consider that AI for exclusion and removal.210 The prohibition should include a narrow and transparent waiver process for research, evaluation, testing, and defensive cybersecurity work. A prohibition is only as effective as an agency’s ability to see what is running on its networks. Congress should therefore codify and modernize CISA’s CDM program so that it provides agencies with continuous discovery and inventory of AI systems, models, and agents, identification of unauthorized or unapproved AI deployments, adversarial testing of AI systems before and after deployment, and supply chain risk management for high-risk vendors, models, and software components. These capabilities would allow CISA and agencies to identify PRC- developed models and their derivatives wherever they appear in federal civilian systems, including models embedded in commercial products several layers below what an agency can readily see. Federal contractors should be held to the same standard. Congress should prohibit contractors from using PRC-developed models in the performance of federal contracts or in information systems that process, store, or transmit federal information. Congress has already taken this approach for DeepSeek, barring Department of War contractors from using it in the performance of their contracts, and federal acquisition rules apply the same scope to TikTok.211 This requirement should take effect first for the largest contractors, those whose annual federal contract obligations exceed a threshold set in statute, and extend to all contractors after a defined transition period, with additional time and technical assistance for small businesses. The same narrow waiver process should apply, consistent with the waivers Congress authorized for DeepSeek.212 During the transition, contractors that use PRC-developed models in covered systems should disclose that use to the contracting agency and maintain a plan to replace those models within a defined period. Those plans should account for a PRC government decision to restrict access, a material change in license terms, discovery of a serious vulnerability or hidden behavior, and new U.S. legal restrictions.213 These restrictions depend on a clear definition of a PRC-developed model. The definition should cover models whose original weights were trained by an entity organized, headquartered, or principally operating in the PRC, or otherwise subject to the jurisdiction or control of the PRC, and models built from those weights through fine-tuning, continued pretraining, merging, or compression. It should not reach an American or allied model solely because some of its training data was generated by a PRC-developed model, although that use should be documented under the provenance standard in Recommendation 3. Developers should also have a way to show that a model is not covered. The same principle should extend to the most sensitive functions of critical infrastructure. Congress should prohibit the use of PRC-developed AI models, including their derivatives, in high-risk functions of critical infrastructure. High- risk functions should be defined narrowly, in coordination with sector risk management agencies, and should focus on uses where a compromised or manipulated model could cause physical harm or disrupt essential services. These include AI agents with access to operational technology, industrial control and safety systems, and tools that write or review code deployed in those environments. The prohibition should apply immediately to new deployments in those functions. Owners and operators already using PRC-developed models in those functions should identify them to their sector risk management agency and to CISA and remove them on a defined schedule. That information should receive the protections Congress provided for reports under CIRCIA, described in Recommendation 8. Where no trusted alternative yet exists, DHS, acting through CISA, should be able to grant an exception based on a CAISSI evaluation of the specific model and on compensating controls, such as running the model only on infrastructure the operator controls, isolating it from systems it does not need to reach, and requiring human approval before it takes consequential actions. Each evaluation should be conducted once and shared with all owners and operators, so that a utility, hospital, or water system does not have to assess the same model on its own. Exceptions should expire on a fixed date and should be reported to Congress. The requirement should be built to work in practice. Removal schedules should account for the availability of trusted alternatives and the time needed to test and certify new systems in safety-critical environments, so that owners and operators are not forced to remove systems faster than they can safely replace them. It should be implemented through sector risk management agencies and existing sector regulators in close coordination with CISA. Congress should provide CAISSI and CISA the resources needed to evaluate models at the pace they are released. A single federal process should be established rather than a patchwork of state and sector rules that would impose different requirements on the same companies.
