blocks.text: C. Share Threat Information and Strengthen Defenses

Recommendation 5. Secure long-term information-sharing authorities and build a developer-level AI threat channel. Any effective public-private response to the risks described in this report depends on the voluntary information-sharing framework established by CISA 2015. Its liability protections, antitrust exemption, and privacy safeguards give companies the legal certainty they need to share cyber threat indicators and defensive measures with DHS and with one another.214 The joint advisory on PRC distillation campaigns specifically called for cross- organization sharing of infrastructure and behavioral indicators among model developers, cloud providers, and API aggregators, and that sharing rests on the protections CISA 2015 provides.215 Since the law’s original authorization expired on September 30, 2025, it has lapsed once and has otherwise been sustained only through a series of short-term extensions, most recently through December 11, 2026.216 Short-term extensions create uncertainty for the companies whose participation the framework depends on, at the very moment the AI threat environment demands more sharing, not less. The Committees’ first priority relating to AI cyber threats is therefore a long- term reauthorization of CISA 2015 through the WIMWIG Act. The Committee on Homeland Security approved the WIMWIG Act by a vote of 25 to 0 on September 3, 2025,217 and the House passed it on July 22, 2026, as part of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027.218 The WIMWIG Act would extend these authorities for ten years and make targeted updates to reflect changes in technology and cybersecurity practice since 2015.219 Congress should enact it without delay. A durable reauthorization should be prioritized, so that industry and government partners have the stability they need. Once long-term authorities are in place, Congress should examine whether the law’s existing definitions reach the threats to AI systems that matter most to national security. Many of those threats, including the theft of model weights, the compromise of AI development infrastructure, malicious activity by AI agents, and the use of fraudulent accounts and proxy networks to extract model capabilities, involve unauthorized activity on information systems and may already fall within the law’s definitions of cyber threat indicators and defensive measures.220 Where they do not, any update should be narrow and targeted. It should be limited to sharing information about malicious actors, their methods, and the measures used to stop them, and it should preserve the law’s existing privacy safeguards and its requirement that sharing serve a cybersecurity purpose. Congress should also complete a long-term reauthorization of the SLCGP, which CISA administers with the Federal Emergency Management Agency.221 The House passed the PILLAR Act on November 17, 2025, which would reauthorize SLCGP and expand its scope to address AI systems and operational technology.222 State, local, tribal, and territorial governments face the same cost pressures that draw private companies to inexpensive PRC models, often with far fewer resources to evaluate them. Congress should prohibit the use of SLCGP funds to acquire, deploy, or maintain PRC-developed AI models or AI services operated by PRC developers, as federal grant rules already do for covered telecommunications equipment and as Congress has done for drones made by covered foreign entities.223 As a condition of funding, recipients should identify PRC-developed models in grant-supported systems through the cybersecurity plans the program already requires and remove any used in high-risk functions on the schedule described in Recommendation 4.224 Grant funds should be available to replace PRC-developed models with trusted alternatives, and CISA should make clear in program guidance that replacement is an eligible activity. Building on these authorities, Congress should direct DHS, acting through CISA, in coordination with the Intelligence Community, the Department of Commerce, and NIST, to establish a mechanism for sharing timely, actionable information with industry about risks associated with specific AI developers and model families. That information should include indicators of illicit distillation, restricted computing acquisitions, and ties to foreign military or intelligence services, delivered at the lowest classification level possible. This mechanism should build on existing partnerships, including the Joint Cyber Defense Collaborative, and advance the AI Action Plan’s call for DHS to lead an AI Information Sharing and Analysis Center.225 Recommendation 6. Evaluate PRC models systematically, translate the results into guidance, and give the Information Technology Sector a single accountable federal partner. Congress should direct CAISSI to evaluate leading PRC-developed models on a recurring basis, including for safeguard robustness, offensive cyber capability, and context-triggered behaviors such as degraded code security when a user identifies with the U.S. government. CISA should translate those evaluations into practical guidance for federal agencies and critical infrastructure owners and operators, developed with sector risk management agencies.226 That guidance should advise owners and operators against deploying PRC-developed models in sensitive functions, set clear expectations for moving off models already in use as trusted alternatives become available, and specify the minimum controls expected for any use that continues in the meantime. These evaluations would also inform the exceptions described in Recommendation 4. Guidance should address both closed and open models and should advise owners and operators to confirm that the AI services and routing services they use do not send their data to infrastructure operated by PRC developers.227 Congress should also codify DHS, acting through CISA, as the Sector Risk Management Agency for the Information Technology Sector, with responsibilities that expressly include AI models and systems, AI compute infrastructure and data centers, cloud services, and software distribution, including open-source repositories. A codified role would give AI developers, cloud providers, and model repositories a single accountable federal partner for threat information, voluntary assessments, and incident coordination. Recommendation 7. Prepare DHS and CISA to defend at machine speed and secure AI agents on federal networks. The cyber threat environment is entering a new phase. Open-weight models capable of autonomously building end-to-end cyber exploits are now available to anyone who downloads them.228 Other nations are already confronting the results. In October 2026, South Korean authorities opened an investigation into cyberattacks on several of the country’s largest banks, one of which exposed the personal credit information of about 25,000 customers, after the country’s president said there were signs that AI models had been used.229 The United States should expect a near future in which cyberattacks are planned, executed, and adapted by AI agents in minutes rather than months, and in which the volume and speed of attacks exceed what human defenders alone can manage.230 Defending federal networks and critical infrastructure in that environment will require defenders who can operate at the same speed, using AI to hunt for threats, detect intrusions, and respond to incidents as they unfold. The expertise needed to build and deploy those capabilities resides largely in the private sector, where frontier AI developers and cybersecurity companies are often months or years ahead of the government in understanding how these systems are built, how they behave, and how they are attacked.231 The federal government cannot close that gap through traditional hiring alone. Congress should establish a time-limited pilot program within DHS that uses direct-hire authority and temporary private sector detailees to bring experienced AI and emerging technology professionals into the Department, with a dedicated allocation for CISA, strong ethics and conflict-of-interest safeguards, and regular reporting to Congress. These professionals would help DHS and CISA evaluate models, detect illicit distillation, inform acquisition decisions, and apply AI to threat hunting, detection, and incident response across federal civilian networks and in support of critical infrastructure owners and operators. They would also transfer their knowledge to the career workforce so that it remains in the Department after their service ends. As agencies deploy AI agents to defend their networks and deliver services, those agents will themselves become targets. Congress should direct CISA to serve as the operational lead for securing AI agents on federal civilian information systems. Agencies should be able to discover every AI agent operating on their networks, assign each one a durable identity and an accountable owner, limit its access to what its task requires, log its actions, and halt it immediately if it deviates from its assigned scope. Agencies should also verify the integrity of the models, tools, and software components that an agent loads or invokes, which would help detect PRC-developed models introduced through third-party agent platforms. These requirements should specify security outcomes rather than particular technologies or vendors. Recommendation 8. Make CISA the single point of submission for AI- related cyber incident reports and establish an independent board to investigate significant incidents. The federal government too often learns of significant AI-related cyber incidents from company blog posts, press reports, or voluntary disclosures, sometimes weeks or months after they occur.232 Frontier AI developers and cybersecurity companies are frequently the first to detect these events, including the theft or attempted theft of model weights, the compromise of AI development and deployment infrastructure, AI agents that access systems without authorization, AI-enabled intrusions, and coordinated foreign efforts to extract model capabilities.233 That information is most valuable in the hands of the agency that can act on it quickly. CISA can use it to warn other potential victims, share indicators across federal networks and critical infrastructure, and coordinate a defensive response.234 PRC-developed models make timely reporting both more important and harder to achieve. The PRC developers whose models are examined in this report are located outside the United States and, once their open weights are downloaded, have no ongoing relationship with the American companies that use them.235 They are beyond the reach of any U.S. reporting requirement and have no incentive to report problems with their models to the U.S. government. The entities positioned to detect incidents involving PRC-developed models are American ones. When a company’s systems are compromised through a PRC-developed model it has deployed, whether through a hijacked AI agent, insecure code the model generated, or behavior the company did not anticipate, the company itself is best placed to identify the model involved. Cloud and inference providers that host these models, and cybersecurity companies that respond to intrusions, see these incidents as well. An effective reporting framework must draw on those entities. Congress has already established that framework. CIRCIA places reporting obligations on the entities that experience significant cyber incidents.236 It directs CISA to require covered entities to report covered cyber incidents within 72 hours and ransom payments within 24 hours, permits supplemental reports as an investigation develops, and allows third parties, such as incident response firms, to submit reports on an entity’s behalf.237 It also provides that reports may not be used to regulate the reporting entity or as evidence against it, exempts them from public disclosure, and preserves legal privileges.238 As Congress considers how the federal government should learn about AI-related incidents, including those involving PRC-developed models, it should build on CIRCIA rather than create new reporting requirements that would ask the same companies to evaluate the same events against different standards, report them to different agencies, and meet different deadlines. AI-related cyber incidents should be reported once, to CISA, under CIRCIA. Congress should ensure that CIRCIA captures significant AI-related cyber incidents without stretching it beyond its purpose. As CISA finalizes its rule, it should confirm that substantial cyber incidents involving AI systems are covered.239 These include the theft or exfiltration of model weights, the compromise of AI training or inference infrastructure, unauthorized access to systems by an AI agent, and intrusions carried out with AI. CISA should also confirm that frontier AI developers and large AI infrastructure providers are covered entities within the Information Technology Sector. Reports should indicate whether an AI system operated by the reporting entity was involved in the incident and, if so, the name of the model’s developer, whether its weights were publicly available, and whether the developer was an entity subject to the control of a foreign adversary. Where the reporting entity has reason to believe an attacker used a particular AI system, the report should include that information as well. Over time, these reports would give the government a picture it does not have today of the role PRC-developed models play in incidents affecting the United States. If the final rule leaves any of these questions unresolved, Congress should address them through targeted amendments to CIRCIA. Reporting tells the government that an incident occurred. Understanding why it occurred requires investigation. The Hugging Face incident, the PRC state- sponsored campaign that used an American AI system to conduct a largely autonomous espionage operation, and the industrial-scale distillation campaigns described in this report each raised questions about root causes that no single company or agency was positioned to answer comprehensively.240 Congress should establish within CISA an independent, nonregulatory board with the authority to review significant cyber incidents and cyber incidents involving AI, determine their root causes, and disseminate lessons learned to critical infrastructure owners and operators, state and local governments, industry, and federal agencies. Reviews of AI-related incidents should examine whether the AI system involved had publicly available weights, whether it was developed by an entity subject to the control of a foreign adversary, whether its safeguards had been removed or altered, and how it was distributed and made available in the United States. The board’s scope should include coordinated efforts by foreign adversaries to extract the capabilities of American AI systems. The board should have no authority to assign liability, and its membership should be balanced and free of foreign conflicts of interest.

blocks.text: D. Impose Costs on Illicit Extraction

Recommendation 9. Hold illicit distillers accountable and close the gray market. Illicit distillation allows PRC developers to take capabilities that American companies spent billions of dollars to build and offer them back to the market at a fraction of the price. The executive branch should impose sanctions on PRC AI developers that the government determines have engaged in industrial-scale illicit distillation or other malicious cyber-enabled activity against American AI companies.241 The Department of the Treasury already has authority to sanction foreign persons responsible for cyber-enabled misappropriation of trade secrets for commercial or competitive advantage.242 The Protecting American Intellectual Property Act separately authorizes sanctions for significant theft of trade secrets belonging to United States persons.243 Those authorities should be applied wherever the conduct meets their standards. Designations should also reach the transfer stations and fraudulent account brokers that the joint advisory identified as sustaining these campaigns.244 The executive branch should use the Entity List and information and communications technology supply chain authorities to restrict designated firms’ access to American chips and computing resources. Each designation should identify the specific conduct at issue, so that it can withstand legal challenge and make clear to industry what conduct triggers it. The executive branch should also account for American companies that depend on affected model families and provide notice and reasonable transition periods where appropriate, consistent with Recommendation 4. Congress should examine whether existing trade secret and computer fraud statutes adequately address unauthorized extraction of model capabilities. That review should include whether model outputs and reasoning obtained in violation of a provider’s terms of service fall within those statutes. The Department of Commerce, working with DHS and industry, should develop identity verification standards for providers of frontier AI services and cloud computing to help close the gray market of proxy “transfer stations” that enable distillation.245 DHS, through CISA, should support cross-industry sharing of distillation indicators, as the joint advisory recommends.246 Recommendation 10. Examine sales of American training data to PRC AI laboratories. Congress should direct the Department of Commerce, in consultation with the Department of War, DHS, and the Intelligence Community, to assess the scale and national security implications of sales by American data vendors to PRC AI laboratories, particularly those on the Entity List or designated under Section 1260H, and to consider the imposition of disclosure requirements, licensing, or export controls on specific categories of expert training data.247

blocks.text: E. Set Durable Rules and Work with Allies

Recommendation 11. Govern both closed and open models and avoid overregulation. Congress should ensure that federal policies, guidance, and programs aimed at securing AI consider the different ways closed and open models are developed and deployed. Congress should also establish a federal baseline for AI transparency and security that provides consistent national rules and does not overburden startups, researchers, or nonprofits. Recommendation 12. Work with allies and deepen understanding of PRC strategy. The executive branch should expand joint model evaluations with allied AI security institutes, building on the joint United States and United Kingdom assessment of Kimi K3, and should work with allies to shape international standards for model provenance and security.248 Congress should direct the Intelligence Community, including the DHS Office of Intelligence and Analysis, to provide the relevant committees with an assessment of PRC government involvement in the open-weight strategies of PRC AI developers, including state financing, direction, and access to model weights and user data.

blocks.text: CONCLUSION

The question before Congress and the entire federal government is not whether Americans should have access to powerful, affordable AI. They should. The question is whether the AI that powers American businesses, public services, and critical infrastructure will be developed by companies accountable to American law and values, or by companies that must answer to the CCP. The record assembled by the Committees shows that PRC-developed models have become embedded in American products faster than companies, customers, or the government have been able to understand the implications. That adoption was driven by real advantages in price and flexibility. Those advantages were built in part on capabilities taken from American developers and sustained by state support and a willingness to lose money for market share. The PRC government has made clear that it views open-weight AI as a source of international influence, and it has already considered restricting access to the models on which others now depend.249 The United States still has time to change this trajectory. American developers retain the lead at the frontier, and a new generation of American open-weight models is emerging.250 The Committees’ recommendations are designed to accelerate that progress, give companies and the government the information they need, keep PRC models out of the systems where the stakes are highest, impose costs on theft, and prepare for disruptions before they occur. The nation should not wait for another rip-and-replace program to learn the lesson of Huawei, ZTE, and DJI a third time. The Committees will continue their oversight of these issues.

Annex A. Zhipu and the PLA Cyberspace Force Information made available to the Committees describes a relationship between elements of the PRC’s military intelligence apparatus and Zhipu.251 According to that information, individuals associated with the 1st Bureau of the PLA Cyberspace Force have been present on multiple occasions at Zhipu’s headquarters in Beijing, most recently in August 2026.252 The 1st Bureau, formerly part of the PLA Strategic Support Force’s Network Systems Department, is understood to conduct signals intelligence, cyber espionage and attack, electronic warfare, and psychological operations, and is believed to be co-located with the PLA Cyberspace Force headquarters.253 The Committees assess with moderate confidence that this pattern indicates a channel between the PLA’s cyber intelligence apparatus and a leading commercial PRC AI developer.254 Annex B. State Support for Chinese AI Developers In addition to the direct grants, state investment, and government ownership described above, China’s AI labs benefit from a broader set of provincial, municipal, and district policies that reduce the cost of compute, deployment, taxes, and talent while also subsidizing customer adoption. Compute subsidies target one of the largest recurring costs of model development. At the provincial level, Zhejiang covers 10 to 30 percent of compute costs for Alibaba and a Zhipu affiliate,255 while Guizhou reimbursed $160,000 for Moonshot’s Kimi model.256 At the municipal level, Beijing discounts compute for Zhipu,257 Moonshot,258 and MiniMax,259 while Hangzhou allocates $37.3 million annually in compute vouchers.260 At the district level, Shanghai’s Xuhui District, where MiniMax is based, offers compute subsidies of up to $3 million annually,261 Beijing’s Haidian District targets Zhipu262 and Moonshot263 with vouchers, and Hangzhou’s Gongshu District provides up to $746,000 for DeepSeek.264 To stimulate adoption, governments also subsidize customers and direct demand toward domestic providers. At the municipal level, Beijing channels subsidized purchases to Alibaba Cloud265 and ByteDance’s Volcano Engine,266 including about $121,000 and $854,000, respectively, in reimbursements for large model applications.267 At the district level, Beijing’s Haidian District also provided Zhipu with a $7.5 million customer voucher pool.268 Elsewhere, Hangzhou funded $750,000 in “AI+” projects,269 while Shanghai state platforms connected MiniMax with industry partners for testing and deployment.270 China’s AI labs also benefit from preferential tax treatment that lowers scaling costs. Qualifying subsidiaries of Moonshot,271 ByteDance,272 MiniMax,273 Zhipu,274 and Alibaba275 receive a 15 percent high tech enterprise tax rate instead of the standard 25 percent.276 Alibaba receives additional multi-year exemptions and, for qualifying entities, a 10 percent Key Software Enterprise rate,277 while Zhipu receives a 100 percent R&D super-deduction.278 Additionally, local governments directly subsidize recruitment, housing, and retention to lower talent costs for key firms. In Beijing, Haidian District provides AI workers up to $225 monthly in rent subsidies alongside targeted hiring programs for Moonshot and ByteDance.279 In Hangzhou, the city offers up to $750,000 for top innovation teams and collaborates with Alibaba on recruitment,280 while Gongshu District deployed a dedicated task force for DeepSeek.281 In Shanghai, Xuhui District enrolled MiniMax in a district training alliance connecting the firm directly to university pipelines.282
